To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the HMM-based labelling of Czech speech is very accurate for read speech, and that the accuracy of the labeller may depend on the speaker's performance.

1) HMM labelling of read connected speech is more precise for good speakers than for poor speakers; 2) HMM-based labelling of read speech is more precise when the labeller uses the whole utterance, not just the phone context, as the input; and 3) HMM-based phone context labelling is more precise than phone transition context labelling.

(1) the HMM labelling of good speakers is less accurate than the labelling of poor speakers, and (2) the labelling accuracy of good speakers is more stable than the labelling accuracy for poor speakers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: can the HMM-based labelling be used for a reliable and efficient assessment of the quality of speech production in a given speaking situation?

the following issues: - the effect of speaker quality on the labeller's performance, - the effect of the labelling mode on the labeller’s performance, - the comparison of impressionistic and automatic labelling.
the question of how to improve the HMM labelling process, and how to make it more robust and reliable for a wide range of speakers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HMM-based labelling is not only useful in terms of the labeller's performance and precision, but it also has the potential to provide information about the speaker's quality of speech production.

, in the given conditions, the HMM labelling of read connected speech was more precise than that of spontaneous speech and that the HMM-based labelling was not equally precise for good and poor speakers, at least in certain conditions.
the HMM-based labeller is a useful tool for the analysis of read connected speech.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HMM-based labeller, in its current form, is not able to distinguish good and poor speakers.
the labelling precision is not only a question of the quality of the labeller, but it is also dependent on the quality of the speaker.
, in general, the HMM labelling is more accurate for the group of better speakers, and for the group with poor performance it is more accurate for a certain mode.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HMM-based labelling is not an easy task.
the HMM labeler can be used to evaluate the speech quality of the speaker and that the evaluation can be done in a way that is not too different from the human evaluation.
HMM-based labelling of phone units is not a straightforward process and that it should be approached with a great caution, especially in case of a large number of different speakers.
